title: Service Mesh: Sidecars, mTLS and When It Pays Off
objectives: Describe the data plane and control plane of a service mesh
Explain how mesh mTLS gives each call a verifiable workload identity
Spot retry and timeout conflicts between the app and the mesh, and judge when a mesh is worth its cost

cards.title: Networking moved out of the app
cards.body: A service mesh puts a proxy in the path of every call between services: a sidecar container next to each workload, or a shared proxy per node. The proxies form the data plane and handle encryption, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and metrics the same way for every language. A control plane sends them configuration and certificates. Proxies keep using their last configuration if the control plane is briefly unavailable.

cards.title: One call through the mesh
cards.body: The app sends a plain request; both proxies do the rest.
steps: The app calls another service by name over a plain local connection
Its proxy picks a healthy endpoint and applies the timeout and retry policy
The proxy opens mutual TLS to the destination proxy with a short-lived workload certificate
The destination proxy checks the caller’s identity against the authorisation policy
It forwards the request to the destination app on the local host
Both proxies emit metrics and trace spans for the call

cards.title: Worked example: retries in two layers multiply
cards.body: The app retries a failed call twice, and the mesh is also set to retry twice. One user request can now reach the downstream service (1 + 2) × (1 + 2) = 9 times. During an outage that becomes nine times the load on a struggling dependency. Decide which layer owns retries, make the inner layer’s total time fit inside the outer deadline, and cap retries with a budget.

cards.title: What mTLS adds over a firewall rule
cards.body: A network rule says which addresses may connect. Mesh mTLS says which workload is calling: each proxy holds a certificate naming its service identity, issued and rotated by the control plane, often every few hours. Policies can then allow “orders may call payments” whatever pod addresses either side has, and every connection inside the cluster is encrypted.

cards.title: Trap: a mesh for three services
cards.body: Every sidecar costs CPU and memory, adds a hop of latency, and the mesh brings its own upgrades and failure modes. For a handful of services in one language, a shared client library and platform-level TLS may do the job. A mesh pays off with many services, several languages, and a requirement for uniform mTLS, traffic control and telemetry.

questions.prompt: In a sidecar mesh, what actually carries a request from one service to another?

choices.label: The control plane, which forwards each request
The cluster DNS server, which relays the call
The proxies running next to each workload
The ingress gateway at the edge of the cluster

questions.explanation: The sidecar proxies are the data plane. The control plane only configures them, DNS only resolves names, and the ingress gateway handles traffic entering the cluster.

questions.prompt: The mesh control plane is down for ten minutes. What happens to calls between running services?

choices.label: They stop, because each call needs control-plane approval
They keep flowing with the last configuration the proxies received
They fall back to plain text with no encryption
They are rerouted through the ingress gateway

questions.explanation: Proxies are statically stable on their last config; new config, new workloads and certificate rotation wait until the control plane returns. Calls are not approved one by one, not downgraded, and not sent through the gateway.

questions.prompt: What does mesh mTLS give that a network firewall rule alone does not?

choices.label: Faster connections, because encryption is moved to hardware
Each call carries a verified workload identity that policy can check
Protection against bugs in the application’s own business logic
Validation of every request body against a published schema

questions.explanation: mTLS proves which workload is calling, so policy can use identities instead of addresses. It adds some cost rather than speed, and it does not inspect business logic or request bodies.

questions.prompt: The app gives each call a 2,000 ms deadline. The mesh may make up to 3 tries in total for that call. What is the longest per-try timeout that keeps all three tries inside the app deadline?
assumptions: Retries start immediately, with no backoff
Every try runs to its full timeout
questions.explanation: Design implication: a 1,000 ms per-try timeout would need 3,000 ms, so the app abandons the call during the third try, and a 2,000 ms per-try timeout makes the mesh retries pointless.

questions.prompt: Which situation most justifies adopting a service mesh?

choices.label: Three services in one language that already share a client library
Hundreds of services in several languages that all need mTLS
A single monolith behind one external load balancer
A nightly batch job that reads files and writes a report

questions.explanation: Uniform mTLS and telemetry across many services and languages is where a mesh saves the most work. A few same-language services can share a library, and a monolith or a batch job has few service-to-service calls to manage.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when one service calls another through the mesh.

items.label: Proxies set up mutual TLS with workload certificates
The request reaches the destination app
The app sends a plain request to the service name
The destination proxy authorises the caller
The local proxy picks an endpoint and applies policy

questions.explanation: Plain locally, policy at the source proxy, mTLS between proxies, authorisation at the destination, then the app.

flashcards.back: Proxies carry traffic; the control plane configures them and issues certificates.
They multiply: (1 + app retries) × (1 + mesh retries). Let one layer own retries.

flashcards.front: When is a mesh worth it?
flashcards.back: Many services, several languages, and a need for uniform mTLS, traffic control and telemetry.

mechanism.title: How a service mesh handles each call
steps: In the classic design, each pod gets a sidecar proxy, and traffic in and out of the app is redirected through it, usually by network rules set up when the pod starts. Newer designs move some work to a shared proxy per node and add per-service proxies only where layer-7 features are needed, which cuts the per-pod cost. Either way the app speaks plain HTTP or gRPC to a local proxy and needs no mesh library.

The control plane watches the cluster for services and endpoints, turns routing, retry and security policies into proxy configuration, and pushes it out. It also acts as a certificate authority: each workload gets a short-lived certificate that encodes its service identity, rotated on a schedule. Proxies cache their configuration, so a control-plane outage stops changes and the setup of new workloads, but existing traffic keeps flowing.

Between proxies, connections use mutual TLS. Both sides present certificates, so the destination proxy knows which workload is calling and can enforce policies such as “only the orders service may call payments, and only with POST”. That moves service-to-service authorisation from IP-based firewall rules, which break as pods move, to identities that follow the workload.

Traffic policy is where meshes help and hurt. Timeouts, retries with budgets, outlier detection that ejects failing endpoints, and weighted traffic splits for canaries are applied the same way for every service. But they stack with whatever the application already does: two layers of retries multiply attempts, and mesh retries that need longer than the app’s overall deadline are retries nobody waits for. Decide which layer owns each behaviour.

The costs are real. Every proxy reserves CPU and memory, which across hundreds of pods adds up to whole machines. Each call takes extra hops through two proxies, adding latency that should be measured rather than assumed. The mesh itself must be upgraded, monitored and debugged, and a bad policy push can break many services at once. Adopt it when uniform security, traffic control and telemetry are worth that operating load.

useWhen: Many services in several languages that need mTLS, consistent telemetry and traffic control.
Zero-trust requirements where calls must be authorised by workload identity.
avoidWhen: Avoid for a few services or a monolith, where a shared library or platform TLS is simpler.
Avoid adopting it only for metrics that existing instrumentation already provides.

rows: Retries and metrics in one language
Less per-pod cost; one proxy shared per node

numbers.title: What the sidecars cost
assumptions: 400 pods, each with a sidecar requesting 0.1 vCPU and 64 MiB
Illustrative request sizes; measure your own proxies
steps: CPU: 400 × 0.1 = 40 vCPU reserved for proxies.
Memory: 400 × 64 MiB = 25,600 MiB, which is 25 GiB.
With 8-vCPU nodes, 40 ÷ 8 = 5 whole nodes’ worth of CPU goes to the mesh.
numbers.result: At scale the mesh costs several machines; that is fine if it replaces work every team would otherwise do, and wasteful if it does not.

india.title: Provider guidance on meshes
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s AKS documentation describes a service mesh as adding capabilities such as traffic management, mTLS-based security and observability, and suggests evaluating your requirements before adopting one. Google Cloud Service Mesh documentation describes a managed control plane that configures proxies for traffic management, mutual TLS and telemetry. Both present the mesh as an option with an operating cost, not a default.

pitfalls.trap: “A mesh makes services reliable because it retries everything.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d let one layer own retries with a budget, because app and mesh retries multiply load during an outage.”

pitfalls.trap: “We need a mesh for our three services.”
pitfalls.say: “For three services in one language I’d start with a shared client and platform TLS, and revisit a mesh as we grow.”

takeaways: Proxies are the data plane; the control plane configures them and issues certificates.
Mesh mTLS gives each call a verified workload identity for policy.
App and mesh retries multiply; one layer should own them.
A mesh pays off with many services and languages, not with a few.

interactive.title: Two timeouts, one hung dependency
interactive.prompt: The app gives each call to the inventory service a 2 s deadline. The mesh retries a failed or slow call up to 3 times in total, with 1 s per try. Inventory hangs completely.

choices.label: The app gives up at 2 s while the mesh starts its third try, which adds load nobody waits for
choices.feedback: Right: the mesh needs up to 3 s, the app waits only 2 s, so the outer deadline ends first.

choices.label: The user waits about 3 s while the mesh finishes all three tries
choices.feedback: The app’s own 2 s deadline ends the request before the mesh is done.

choices.label: The user gets an error after 1 s, when the first mesh try times out
choices.feedback: The mesh retries after the first try instead of returning the error.

interactive.reveal: Make the inner layer’s total time fit inside the outer deadline, for example 2 tries of 0.8 s, or let only one layer retry.
